summary:
Tayf is a web tool that tells space teams where on Earth, and in which month, to test Moon and Mars equipment. Teams still pick analog test sites by experience. NASA’s 2024 Artemis moonwalk rehearsal in Arizona, for example, used a spotlight to imitate the lunar Sun. We found no public tool that ranks sites for a given test and month.

Tayf scores every land cell on Earth against a target (Jezero crater or a lunar base ridge) for five NASA test types. It uses NASA POWER climatology and Perseverance’s MEDA weather data. Each site card shows the numbers behind its score, such as Sun elevation and day-to-night ground temperature. It also shows what Earth can’t match, such as gravity, thin air and radiation.

To check the estimates, we built a low-cost ESP32 sensor pod that mirrors Perseverance’s weather station. It already streams live to our website, and next it will log 24 hours at a Qatar sabkha for comparison with the satellite data.
details:
What it does. Tayf helps teams choose a place on Earth to test Moon and Mars equipment. The user picks a target (Jezero crater or a lunar base ridge), a test type (five NASA test types, from mobility to power) and a month. Tayf then scores every land cell on Earth, 68,816 of them for one Mars power test in January. Each site gets a card that sets Earth’s numbers beside the target’s. Examples are the highest Sun angle, the share of daylight with the Sun below 10°, the horizon the Sun sweeps, and the day-to-night ground temperature swing. Each condition gets its own score, and these combine into an overall match. Gravity, thin air, space radiation and the 29.5-day lunar day are never scored. They are always shown, so users see where Earth fails.

How it works. Earth-side values come from NASA POWER climatology (2001–2025). Mars-side values come from Perseverance’s MEDA weather station, via the NASA Planetary Data System. The site is a web app with a map page, site cards and a live data panel.

Hardware. A satellite-based estimate is still an estimate, so we built a sensor pod to check it. An ESP32 (NodeMCU-32S) reads sensors that mirror Perseverance’s weather station: infrared ground temperature, up- and down-facing light, UV, pressure (BMP180), air temperature and humidity (DHT11), and a DS18B20 soil probe. The enclosure is 3D-printed and designed in SolidWorks. The pod already streams live to the website. Next it will log 24 hours at a Qatar sabkha for comparison with the satellite estimate. The hardware shows that the software’s inputs can be measured on the ground.

Benefits and impact. Test teams get a ranked, explained shortlist of sites instead of choosing by experience. Students and university rover teams use it free. Space companies could later buy site reports, and pods placed at candidate sites would let teams measure before they travel. Each pod costs under 200 QAR in parts [confirm after the sensor changes].

What’s creative. Existing tools, such as NASA’s Analog Explorer, ESA’s catalogue and Europlanet’s sites, list or show analog sites. None ranks them for a specific test and month. Tayf also shows its limits openly.

Factors we considered. We kept scores tied to measurable data. We stated where Earth can’t match the target. We also marked field-log charts as simulated until real data exists.
